# Textbooks

We do not have a single required textbook for this course. Instead, our primary course materials will be the **Thinking with Data** notebooks, supplemented by selected readings from several freely available online texts.

You will occasionally be assigned specific chapters or sections from these books. You are not expected to read any of them cover-to-cover, but they are also excellent references when you would like another explanation of a topic, more examples, or additional practice.

- [Computational and Inferential Thinking: The Foundations of Data Science](https://inferentialthinking.com/) —
  the textbook developed for Berkeley's Data 8 course and one of the inspirations for this course. It provides an excellent introduction to thinking with data, visualization, sampling, and statistical inference. Note that Data 8 uses its own `datascience` Python package; in this course, we will instead use `pandas` and other widely used Python data-science tools.

- [Python Data Science Handbook](https://jakevdp.github.io/PythonDataScienceHandbook/) —
  Jake VanderPlas's introduction to scientific computing and data science with Python. It is a useful resource for NumPy, pandas, visualization, and other tools we will encounter throughout the semester.

- [Python for Data Analysis](https://wesmckinney.com/book/) —
  Wes McKinney's guide to data analysis with Python. McKinney is the creator of pandas, and this book is an excellent resource when you want to understand pandas in greater depth.

- [Think Stats](https://greenteapress.com/wp/think-stats-2e/) —
  Allen Downey's introduction to statistics using Python. We will draw on it especially later in the course as we begin thinking about distributions, sampling, uncertainty, and statistical reasoning.
